titles.title: Advanced technology to enhance monitoring of dairy cow health
Use of advanced technology to enhance monitoring of dairy cow health

descriptions.description: The UK trend of increasing dairy herd size and milk yield per cow has generated challenges for dairy farmers, namely in the realm of cow health and herd management. Technology has the potential to facilitate livestock production, however the uptake of cow monitoring technologies within the UK has not been widely researched. There are key periods within the life of a cow where high levels of cow monitoring are required, for example calving, and technology has the potential to aid farmers with cow management. Calving cows require regular observation as it is a period of high risk for cow and calf; two common issues at calving are calving difficulty (dystocia) and calf mortality. However as average herd size increases, farm staff are under pressure to manage their time effectively and calving presents a management challenge. In the period surrounding calving, cows are susceptible to a range of disorders such as hypocalcaemia – a metabolic disorder which can be fatal. Automated systems could be used to detect calving and clinical hypocalcaemia on commercial dairy farms to help facilitate herd management and improve cow health and welfare. The first study was a survey investigating the prevalence and use of automated cow technologies was completed by 122 UK dairy farmers. The results showed that approximately 3 in 5 dairy farmers utilised automated cow monitoring technology, and the main parameters that were monitored on UK dairy farms were heat detection, daily milk yield, and illness detection. Half of dairy producers that do not have automated cow monitoring technology installed will invest within the next 5 years, and it is therefore expected that the prevalence of automated cow technologies will increase. Results indicated that dairy producers were satisfied with automated cow monitoring technology on their farms. The main barrier to adoption of technology was initial investment cost. The second study investigated the behavioural changes of eutocic and dystocic dairy cows in late gestation and on the day of calving. An accelerometer was attached to the hind leg of dairy cattle to collect lying and activity behavioural data. Data were collected from 32 multiparous and 12 primiparous Holstein dairy cattle to describe normal calving behavior and parity differences. To quantify behaviour related to calving difficulty, the data from 14 animals that had dystocia at calving were matched to cows that had an eutocic calving based on parity, locomotion score, calf breed, calf sex, month, and year of calving. Retrospective analysis was conducted on lying and activity data in the period before calving (d -4 to d -1) and on the day of calving (d 0). Findings suggest that cow behaviour on the day of calving was significantly different when compared to a non-calving control period (d -4). Important differences were found in the behaviour of primiparous and multiparous cows during the period prior to calving. In addition, the days relative to calving were found to affect activity behaviours. Three different types of machine learning methods (random forest, decision tree, and neural network) were unable to successfully use behavioural changes to classify the day before calving or the 2h period before calving. There was no difference in the behaviour between 14 cows with assisted calvings (dystocic) and 14 cows with non-assisted calvings (eutocic). The third study was designed to describe and quantify any behavioural differences between cows diagnosed with normocalcaemia, subclinical hypocalcaemia, and clinical hypocalcaemia at calving. A total of 51 multiparous cows and 21 primiparous cows were categorised as having either clinical hypocalcaemia, subclinical hypocalcaemia, or normocalcaemia at calving. Lying and activity behaviours of multiparous and primiparous cows within each blood calcium category was assessed for differences. In the 14 d before calving, multiparous cows with normocalcaemia had fewer lying and standing bouts compared to multiparous cows with subclinical hypocalcaemia and clinical hypocalcaemia. In addition, the step count of primiparous cows with normocalcaemia decreased across the period. These results suggested behaviour could be used to categorise cows into blood calcium group categories prior to calving. Cows that had clinical hypocalcaemia at calving were less active and lay down more in the 21 d post-calving. This finding suggests that the effect of hypocalcaemia on cow behaviour was long lasting. Overall, this thesis has shown that the use of remote sensing technology can be used to detect behavioural changes associated with calving and hypocalcaemia. These findings could be used to develop automated detection systems for calving and hypocalcaemia which could aid dairy producers in herd and cow health management. In addition, a survey of UK dairy farmers has shown that farmers are willing to invest in cow monitoring technology and 68% surveyed farmers would invest in the next 5 years. Return on investment was considered the most important criteria when selecting a technology for purchase. Therefore, it is important that technology companies can prove the monetary and non-monetary benefits of technologies.

titles.title: Cattle Physiological Sensor Dataset for Disease Classification and Health Monitoring

descriptions.description:
This dataset was developed to support IoT-based cattle health monitoring and disease classification, containing 10,000 records of physiological, motion, environmental, and biochemical measurements from multiple cattle and farms. The dataset includes the following variables:




Variable
Description




Animal_ID
Identifier of the individual cattle.


Farm_ID
Identifier of the farm.


Temperature_C
Body temperature measurement in degrees Celsius.


Pulse_BPM
Pulse rate in beats per minute.


Accel_X, Accel_Y, Accel_Z
Three-axis accelerometer measurements.


Gyro_X, Gyro_Y, Gyro_Z
Three-axis gyroscope measurements.


MQ_Gas
Measurement obtained from the MQ gas sensor.


Saliva_pH
Saliva pH measurement.


Disease
Disease or health-status label associated with the record.




The disease labels represented in the dataset are Ketosis, Mastitis, Ruminal Bloat, and Healthy.

The dataset is provided in CSV format and can be used independently for academic research, benchmarking, exploratory analysis, and development of intelligent livestock monitoring systems.

titles.title: Monitoring heat stress in dairy cows - Possibilities and limitations

descriptions.description:
In light of projected climate change, the issue of animal welfare and heat stress in dairy cows has become increasingly important. The Temperature-Humidity Index (THI) is the most widely used approach for identifying heat stress; however, this index does not include animal-specific indicators. Therefore, the objective of our research over nearly the past two decades was to analyze physiological and behavioral characteristics of lactating Holstein-Friesian cows under a continental climatic zone in Germany under heat stress. In addition, individual cow-specific factors and various effects of heat stress in relation to climatic conditions were taken into account. In addition to the barn climate (ambient temperature, relative humidity, and THI), the cows’ body temperature, respiratory rate, heart rate, rumination time, as well as activity and lying behavior were analyzed. High-yielding dairy cows show behavioural and physiological reactions under heat stress. However, the severity of heat stress is difficult to quantify. 

Introduction

In the course of a predicted climate change, the problem of welfare and heat load of dairy cows has become increasingly important even under moderate climate conditions. The heat load of cows is commonly assessed using the temperature-humidity index (THI), determined with a combination of ambient temperature and relative humidity (NRC, 1971, Schüller et al., 2013). 

Several studies have shown that THI predictions are currently underestimating the severity of heat stress on physiological responses in dairy cows (West et al., 2003, Zimbelman et al., 2011). Physiological and behavioural parameters, such as respiration rate (RR), heart rate (HR) and lying time, have been demonstrated as adequate and timely indicators of heat stress in dairy cows (Hoffmann et al., 2020, Pinto et al., 2020, Heinicke et al., 2021).

In order to maintain the well-being of cows and their performance, it is important to know when heat load leads to an impairment of physiological parameters such as body temperature and respiration rate.  In the literature it is already possible to identify physiological and ethological responses in animals that correlate with climatic conditions (Herbut et al., 2019, Hoffmann et al., 2020). The challenge lies in identifying the responses that are relevant for assessing individual heat stress as an early warning method. Below, we provide an overview of the current state of knowledge and our own measurements regarding physiological and ethological parameters and their relationship to heat stress. 

Body temperature

The rumen temperature of high yielding dairy cows was measured with a rumen bolus (smaXtec, Graz, Austria) and shows changes under heat stress conditions. The body temperatures of the cows as well as the ambient temperature and relative humidity of the barn were measured every 10 minutes. Based on this two barn parameters the current THI value was calculated according to NRC (1971) as follows:

THI = (1.8 × AT + 32) - (0.55 – 0.0055 × RH) × (1.8 × AT - 26),                   (1)

 where AT is the dry bulb temperature in °C, and RH is the relative humidity in %.

The body temperatures were linked to the ambient temperatures and THI values, and, besides a Spearman`s correlation (ρ), the heat load thresholds were determined using the broken-stick model. There was only a slight positive correlation (P<0.001) between rumen temperatures and ambient temperatures (ρ=0.08) as well as between rumen temperatures and THI (ρ=0.09). The broken-stick model was performed further for every single cow taken the individuality into account. However, it was visible that even at high ambient temperatures, cows were still able to keep their core body temperature relatively constant and that break points in rumen temperature appeared relatively late (ambient temperatures > 20 °C, THI valus > 70).

Respiratory rate

To determine the respiratory rate of the dairy cows, the number of breaths was visually recorded for 30 seconds by counting the right thoracoabdominal movements and multiplied by two (breaths per minute). Depending on the measurement series, these measurements were taken hourly or twice daily (in the morning and in the afternoon). At the same time, it was recorded whether the animal was lying down or standing during the measurement.

Respiratory rate increased with increasing heat stress (p<0.001). The results showed a significant interaction effect between current heat stress intensity and body posture on respiratory rate. The respiratory rate of cows in the lying position was higher than that of standing cows at the same heat stress intensity. In addition, an increase in respiratory rate of 0.23 ± 0.19 breaths per minute was observed for every kilogram of milk produced daily (Pinto et al., 2019).

The THI threshold for heat stress, as related to respiratory rate, was determined for each body posture (standing vs. lying down) during data collection. The results showed two different stress thresholds for heat stress depending on body posture. The best fit for the stress threshold based on respiratory rate was 70 for cows in the standing position, while the model for cows in the lying position showed a lower stress threshold at a THI of 65 (Pinto et al., 2020).

Heart Rate

Heart rate was measured exclusively in standing cows twice daily (in the morning and in the afternoon) using a stethoscope between the fourth and sixth intercostal spaces in the area of the sternum for 15 seconds. The reading was multiplied by four (resulting in beats per minute).

The heart rate response at a heat stress threshold of 69 THI indicated that the animals were initiating adaptations to cope with heat stress (Pinto et al., 2020).

In earlier studies with Holstein dairy cows, heart rate increased at 72 THI (Bohmanova (Bohmanova et al., 2007, Morton et al., 2007) and 68 THI (Zimbelman et al., 2011).

Rumination Time

Rumination time was continuously recorded over 24 hours using a microphone-based rumination sensor (Lely Qwes HR, Lely, Maassluis, NL) attached to each cow’s collar. An additional weight on the collar keeps the rumination sensor in the optimal measurement position, at the top left behind the ear. Data was transmitted during milking via the automatic milking system. The software aggregated the data and reported it in minutes per 2-hour period as well as in minutes per day.

Our study showed that heat stress also has a negative effect on rumination time. Using broken-stick regression, a heat stress threshold of 52 THI was determined, indicating changes in rumination time in lactating dairy cows. Changes in rumination time up to the heat stress threshold were influenced by several cow-specific factors, such as milk yield, parity, stage of lactation, and stage of pregnancy (Müschner-Siemens et al., 2020, Müschner-Siemens et al., 2024). For example, multiparous, high-producing cows in later stages of lactation may be more severely affected than other cows. A negative correlation between rumination time and heat stress exposure has frequently been observed in various studies (Acatincăi et al., 2010, Soriani et al., 2013, Moretti et al., 2017). This was consistent with our results; however, we found an individual threshold for heat stress that is lower in temperate climates than in hotter regions.

Activity and lying behavior

To record individual animal activity and lying behavior, the cows were fitted with an IceTag3DTM accelerometer (IceRobotics, Edinburgh, UK) on their hind legs. The accelerometer contains a position and acceleration sensor that recorded the cow’s posture (lying down vs. standing/walking), the number of steps, and the movement index per second. Based on this data, the duration, frequency, and timing of lying, standing, and walking activities were determined.

It has been shown that cows alter their activity and lying behavior depending on the duration of daily heat exposure that exceeds the threshold for heat stress (Heinicke et al., 2018, Heinicke et al., 2019). An increase in the duration and intensity of heat stress on the measurement day led to a decrease in lying time and an increase in step count. The cows’ behavioral responses to heat stress were less pronounced when the measurement day was preceded by an additional accumulation of heat stress over a three-day period (Heinicke et al., 2019). The decrease in lying time observed under heat stress conditions is consistent with findings in the literature (Cook et al., 2007, Endres and Barberg, 2007, Herbut and Angrecka, 2018).

Conclusions

All parameters have proven to be useful evaluation criteria for assessing the physiological and ethological responses of dairy cows to heat stress. Sensors for activity and rumination recording, already in use in livestock farming, could be valuable tools for herd managers to see early signs of heat stress. Respiratory rate, as visually recorded for individual animals, is a sensitive parameter and offers great potential for real-time monitoring to detect heat stress early. However, visual recordings are extremely time-consuming and therefore difficult to implement in everyday practice. Consequently, algorithms should be developed that process physiological and ethological reactions of the animals in combination and incorporate them into management decisions, so that complex deviations from normal animal behavior serve as warning signals. A key approach for the implementation and application of data-driven decision-making algorithms is the automatic and digital recording of respiratory rate using a sensor, which is currently the focus of intensive research within our working group (Strutzke et al., 2019, Hoffmann et al., 2024).

titles.title: Labeled sensor dataset of beef cattle behavior grazing desert rangelands

descriptions.description: Applications of Precision Livestock Management are widely used in intensive production systems, mainly in pasture-based and conventional feeding operations where animal behavior can differ significantly compared to more extensive grazing systems operating on native rangeland. Few studies involved beef cattle production systems operating on rangelands that apply wireless data transmission and ML analytics in real-time.The objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of multiclass ML models for classification of beef cattle behaviors on arid rangeland pastures. The goal was to develop and deploy a real-time animal monitoring system integrating wearable accelerometers, LoRaWAN wireless transmission, ML analytics and a user-friendly dashboard application. This system would allow innovative approaches for beef cattle management on rangelands focusing on production efficiency, sustainability, and improved animal welfare.A case study was conducted to train and test ML classifiers of animal behavior, specifically designed for beef cows managed on large pastures of arid rangeland. Cattle used in this study were born and raised on their respective ranches, and were well adapted to the climatic, edaphic and vegetation conditions of the Northern Chihuahuan Desert. Mature cows (4-9 years old) were used for behavior observations. Focal cows included six Angus-Hereford crossbreed cows randomly selected from a herd of 25 and six Raramuri Criollo cows selected from a herd of 54 at the Jornada Experimental Range (USDA). Additionally, six Brangus cows were selected from a herd of 27 and six Brahman cows were selected from a herd of 22 at the Chihuahuan Desert Rangeland Research Center (NMSU). All cows were equipped with Compact Trackers (CT).The CTs consisted of a multifunctional tracking device equipped with a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receptor and an embedded triaxial accelerometer sensor. The triaxial accelerometer assessed motion intensity in three dimensions (X, Y, Z). Motion was measured in inertial units at a 12.5 Hz frequency and expressed as g force units. Proprietary onboard processing algorithms summarize the motion data into a one-dimension motion index (MI) aggregated every 1 minute. Cow behavior observation were performed using video recording. All video recordings were reviewed and annotated by the same trained operator and one trained assistant. Annotations included two main motion states, Active (AC) or stationary (ST), two mutually exclusive AC behaviors, walking (WA) and grazing (GR), and two mutually exclusive ST behaviors, ruminating (RU) or resting (RE). AC was considered when cows exhibited horizontal displacement, either while walking with their head up (WA) or grazing with their head down while biting, chewing and searching for forage (GR). ST was considered when cows were either standing still or lying down, either fully resting (RE) or exhibiting gentle head, neck and jaw movements during rumination (RU). Other annotated activities included sleeping, scratching, grooming and nursing. Annotations were summarized to a 1-min interval to match the 1-min sensor MI data. A behavior state or class was annotated if the recorded behavior state or class lasted 30 seconds or more. If the observed behavior lasted less than 30 seconds, the previous label annotation was considered.

titles.title: Goats in a Warming World: Mechanisms of Climate Resilience and Strategies for Sustainable Production

descriptions.description:
Abstract

Goats are well adapted to environmental stress and possess superior thermotolerance potential that enables them to perform under extreme temperatures, limited feed and water availability and other challenging conditions. Their resilience potential is associated with physiological, behavioural and genetic characteristics that allows them to tolerate harsh conditions however, the expression of these traits differs among breeds and individual animals. Among the goat populations, indigenous goat breeds are valuable because of generations of adaptation to local environments have shaped genetic diversity that can contribute to future climate-resilient breeding programs. At the molecular level, genomics and other omics studies are providing insights into the biological and molecular processes associated with these adaptive responses. However, the ability to withstand environmental stress does not always ensure maintenance of production, since increased thermoregulatory demands can alter nutrient partitioning and reduces the resources available for growth, reproduction, milk and meat production. Nutritional and management interventions can help minimize these production losses however, genetic interventions can provide permanent solution by combining adaptive capacity with desirable productive traits over generations. Further, Precision livestock farming (PLF) technologies support this process by enabling continuous monitoring of animal behaviour, physiology and environmental exposure. Such efforts facilitate the identification and selection of goats that remain healthy and productive under climatic stress thereby, strengthening the basis for sustainable production and food security in increasingly variable environments.

Keywords: Climate change; Goats; indigenous breeds; omics technologies; PLF; resilience  

 

1.     Introduction: The Goat as a Climate-Resilient Livestock Species

As the global population continues to grow rapidly, there will be an increasing demand for animal-source foods to ensure the constant food supply to the growing human population. However, climate change is altering the livestock production as the conditions that would favor livestock productivity is becoming hostile. The increasing temperature, reduced availability of water, reduction in grazing land and increased climatic variability significantly impacts the productivity, reproductivity and welfare of animals (Sejian et al., 2018). Under these circumstances, livestock species that have lower requirements but remain productive will be the key players in ensuring global food securityAmong livestock species, goats have remarkable adaptation to climatic conditions as they can survive in different climatic zones including the Sahara Desert where temperatures rise above 45°C, as well as high altitude regions such as the Himalayas above 4,000 meters, tropical rainforest regions and semi-arid drought prone areas (Danso et al., 2024). They play a significant role in contributing to global food security through production of meat, milk, fiber, hides and manure, as well as being an important source of income to millions of poor farmers (Sejian et al., 2018). 

The ability of goats to withstand the harsh climatic changes is due to the fact that they possess unique attributes in terms of morphology, physiology, behavior and genetics. The small body size, thermoregulation capacity, browsing behavior, lower water requirement and their capability to feed on low-quality feed allows goats to remain productive under adverse and limited climatic conditions (Nair et al., 2021). The advancement in next-generation sequencing technologies and omics platforms have played an enormous role in gaining insight into the molecular mechanisms of these adaptation capabilities, which has assisted in identifying the genes and biomarkers for climate-resilient breeding (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). Additionally, integrating with the emerging precision livestock farming enables real-time evaluation of animal health, well-being and environmental reactions, thus leading to more accurate and climate-smart management practices (Rebez et al., 2024). This chapter focuses on the effects of climatic stressors on goat production systems, as well as the biology, genetics, and molecular adaptations in goats that allows them to cope up with the challenging environments. In addition, the chapter discusses the inclusion of indigenous genetic resources, application of multi-omics approaches, precision livestock farming, and climate-smart approaches for formulating a holistic strategy for goat production.

2.     Climate Stressors Shaping the Future of Goat Production

Climate change is modifying the environmental circumstances that have made goat farming successful previously. The increase in ambient temperature, increased and persistent heat waves, irregular precipitation, persistent droughts and extreme weather conditions have become a common phenomenon (Sejian et al., 2018).These changes are not only intensifying thermal stress but are also affecting the availability of feeds and water, vegetation development, and the distribution of pasturelands (Nardone et al., 2010).In many arid and semi-arid areas, climate changes have contributed to desertification, decrease in the availability of food and increase in competition for natural resources.With the intensification of these climate changes even the goats withsuperior adaptive abilityare facing greater challenges in maintaining their health and productivity.

The climatic stressors have significant effects on goat health, well-being and productivity. Among these stressors, heat stress is considered to be the most detrimental affecting the physiological processes by elevating body temperature, respiration rateand water intake while decreasing feed intake and nutrient absorption.Further, long-term heat exposure will adversely affect the growth performance, reproduction, milk productivity, immunity and kid survival rate (Cheng et al., 2022). At the same time, feed shortage caused by drought also results in reduced quantity and quality of pasture, thereby making the goats rely on browsing of poor-quality feed that might fail to satisfy the nutritional needs of the goats.Water scarcity further compounds these problems as it impacts metabolic functions, thermoregulationand the performance of animals.In addition to these direct effects, climate change hinders livestock production through their indirect effects by altering feed resources, grazing ecosystem and the distribution of parasites and infectious diseases (Lacetera et al., 2019).Thus, climatic factors decrease productivity and make goat farming systems more vulnerable especially in the developing countries.

3.     The Biology of Goat Resilience: Why Do Some Goats Cope Better?

Goat’s ability to survive climatic stress differs considerably between breeds, even among the individuals of same breed and production system (Renaudeau et al., 2012).Some goats resist and perform normally in terms of growth, reproduction, milk production and immune system functioning in hot conditions, while other goats fail to resist the climatic conditions and thus their performances deteriorate significantly. This resistance to climatic stress depends on the adaptation ability of these goats, which is influenced by genetics, environmental exposure, physiological plasticity, nutrition and adaptation to the local climatic condition (Sejian et al., 2018). Consequently, indigenous goats are usually more tolerant to climatic stress because they have been evolving for generations in either hot, dry, or mountainous climates and the generations of exposure to the unfavorable environmental condition have allowed positive selection for beneficial alleles and regulatory mechanism that help goats survive under climatic stress (Sejian et al., 2021). Therefore, climate resilience is not a single trait but rather a combination of many biological mechanisms that act together to ensure normal body functioning amid stressful environmental conditions.

The adaptation of goats to climate depends on the combined effect of the physiological, behavioral, endocrine, and molecular processes to counteract the impact of environmental stress. Physiological thermoregulation through sweating, panting, vasodilation of blood vessels and metabolic heat reduction, as well as behavioral adaptation of the animals like seeking for shade and altering grazing behaviour are helpful in thermoregulation. These mechanisms are further aided by efficient water use, feeding of poor quality feedstuffs and metabolic plasticity that enable the goats to maintain their physiological functions despite being exposed to heat and nutritional stresses for a prolonged period (Nair et al., 2021). Hormonal regulation through cortisol and thyroid hormones additionally regulates metabolism in accordance with requirements of the environment, while increased expression of heat shock proteins and antioxidant enzymes ensures protection of cells against oxidative stress, stabilization of proteins, and cell viability (Nair et al., 2021). At the molecular level, these adaptation processes occur through the interplay of several genes that are associated with thermoregulation, immune system, energy balance, hydration and cell maintenance. The expression of these genes are further influenced by several factors like environmental conditions, nutrition, epigenetic mechanisms, host-microbiome relationship and management practices (Abioja et al., 2023). Consequently, these mechanisms define the climate resilience in goats and can be used as a basis for improving breeding, nutrition and farm management.

4.     The Multi-Omics Architecture of Climate Resilience 

Climate resilience in goats cannot be comprehensively understood through research on one particular gene or biological process since each level of biology plays an important role in the adaptation process. Omics technologies have greatly transformed climate resilience studies because of their ability to allow for the analysis of diverse biological elements, including genes, transcripts, proteins, metabolites and microbes. These approaches help gain insights into the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying adaptation thereby, providing a deeper understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying climate resilience. The different layers of omics offer different aspects of the biological puzzle. Genetic variation is one of the key determinants of climate resilience in goats and genomics has been extensively applied to study genes and genomic loci for heat resistance, immune responses, energy metabolism and other climate resilient traits (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). However, the activity of genes undergo constant changes due to environmental stress and transcriptomics has made possible to gain useful information about the genes and pathways regulated in response to stressful conditions (Shashank et al., 2024). The effect of the environment on gene expression has also been studied by epigenomics which revealed epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation, histone modifications and non-coding RNAs are involved in adaptive plasticity without changing the DNA sequence (Aravindh et al., 2025). Similarly, proteomics and metabolomics have increased our knowledge on the functional and metabolic changes related to cellular defense, antioxidative defense, immune system, tissue regeneration and energy metabolism under climatic stress conditions (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). Furthermore, research on the microbiome has emphasized the importance of rumen and gut microflora in increasing the efficiency of nutrition, metabolism, immune response, and methane regulation (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). However, the real strength of these technologies is harnessed through a multi-omics strategy. Multi-omics technology integrates information from the genome, transcriptome, epigenome, proteome, metabolome and microbiome to encompass the complexity of the interaction process during the adaptation process. This can aid in providing a better understanding of climate adaptation mechanisms thereby, identifying biomarkers and pathways that can be used in breeding and management programs (Xiong et al., 2025).

5.     Indigenous Goat Breeds: Nature's Climate-Resilience Laboratory

Indigenous breeds of goats are considered as important genetic pools containing adaptive diversity resulting from thousands of years of selection for survival in diverse agroecological environments.While commercial breeds have mostly been selected under well-managed conditions for their superior production, indigenous goat breeds have been selected in an environment of prolonged heat stress, periodic shortage of feed and water, difficult topography and disease prevalence. This process of natural selection has resulted in selection of goats that could maintain their physiological stability, reproduction and productivity in an environmentally constrained situation.As a result, indigenous goat breeds exhibit a wide range of adaptive characteristics, such as heat resistance, reduced maintenance energy requirements, greater ability to digest low-quality forages, water conservation and disease resistance. Although indigenous goats are often more tolerant of adverse conditions than most commercial goat breeds, the adaptive ability varies widely even among different indigenous breeds (Nair et al., 2021). The adaptive potential of animals varies based on the environment under which each goat breed evolvesresulting in varying thermoregulatory capabilities, metabolic efficiency, endocrine response, immunity and cellular stress resistance.Such breed differences have been established through comparative studies.According to Pragna et al. (2018) there was a notable difference between the growth performance, growth hormone leveland IGF-1 expression among Salem Black, Osmanabadi, and Malabari goats in summer conditions, showing differences in their tolerance towards thermal stress. In a similar study, Aleena et al. (2018) showed better thermos physiological response and better HSP70 expression pattern in Salem Black goats than Osmanabadi and Malabari goats, thereby showing higher cellular protection in case of thermal stress.Such findings indicate the fact that the degree of resilience to climate changes differs between indigenous breeds of goats and depends on their adaptation to local environmental conditions.Consequently, naturally selected adaptive traits in indigenous goats play an essential role in providing genetic base for developing climate resilient production systems. The conservation of these indigenous populations is important for the preservation of the valuable adaptive traits and genetic resources.However, attempts should also be directed towards improving the productive capacity of the breeds without changing their high thermotolerance and adaptability potential.Such an approach will aid in breeding goats that will be both productive and adaptive, thereby guaranteeing sustainable livestock production.

6.     Enhancing Goat Resilience: From Natural Adaptation to Precision Intervention

Natural adaptation is an important basis for resilience however, it may fail to provide adequate resilience if the frequency or intensity of climatic stress continues to increase. Improving resilience thus involves a combination of genetic, nutritional and management approaches that help build on the innate adaptability of the animal (Sejian et al., 2018). Genetic selection programs can be employed in selecting animals that have the ability to withstand heat stresses while having superior growth, milk, meat and reproductive performance (Renaudeau et al., 2012). Nutritional approaches like antioxidants, minerals, phytogenic plants, probiotics, and bioactive feed ingredients can play a key role in maintaining metabolic function, immunity, and ruminal function under stressful conditions. Managemental approaches are equally important and include provision of shade and ventilation, availability of good water, alteration in grazing and feeding times to avoid exposure during the hot periods and altering stocking rates depending on pastures and climate (Prates, 2025). The development of precision technology presents an opportunity for making these interventions timely and animal specific. Wearable sensors, automatic thermal cameras, environment sensors, and digital monitoring tools may constantly monitor the changes in body temperature, respiration, physical activities, consumption of food and water, and the climate conditions surrounding the animals (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). The above data can help detect any early signs of heat stress or other forms of environmental stress even before the onset of any obvious production losses, helping farmers to react by altering the feeding regime, drinking water, providing shade or even rehousing them. Further, when integrated with genetic data and nutritional information, these technologies will aid in making more accurate decisions for both individual animals and entire herds (Idowu and Idowu, 2026).

7.     Digital and Precision Goat Farming: Measuring Resilience in Real Time 

Technological improvements in sensor-based technologies have made it possible to track the changes in behavior and physiological responses of goats in conjunction with the environmental parameters in real time. Continuous monitoring offers a greater chance of understanding the responses and recovery of goats during climatic stress. Wearable accelerometers have been employed to monitor movement and identify different behaviours like grazing, browsing, walking and resting period of the animal. Moreau et al. (2009) illustrated the usage of tri-axial accelerometers for automated identification of grazing behaviour in goats under different production systems. The GPS-based technique gives additional information on the distance of movement, grazing behaviour and location (Chebli et al., 2022). For instance, accelerometers together with GPS has been employed to determine the amount of time spent on grazing by dairy goats, thus highlighting the benefits of this approach in measuring the behaviour response in field conditions. Additionally, the use of infrared thermography gives an additional tool for non-invasive measurement of surface temperature and the environmental sensors provides continuous monitoring of temperature, humidity and heat load. Changes in eye temperature in Blanca Serrana goats have been reported by Bartolomé et al. (2019) during a stressful situation, confirming its potential value as a non-invasive parameter of physiological stress. Emerging technologies like automated video analysis and audio monitoring are also being investigated for continuous measurement of feeding, ruminating, and behavioral characteristics. All these technologies provide for multiple objective recordings, which, in turn, can serve as a tool to help assess an individual’s response to stress factors. Such technologies provide continuous readings which assist in evaluating the response of individual goats to environmental stress. Repetitive observations may further aid in differentiating animals having varying degrees of resilience. Correlating such responses with growth, milk production, reproduction, health and genetics data can enhance the process of selecting goats that retain their productive potential even under stressed climates.

8.     Sustainable Production: Moving Beyond Survival Toward Productivity

Animal's ability to tolerate climatic stressors may not automatically mean sustained productivity.Under heat stress conditions, goats resort to various thermoregulation strategies such as increased respiration rate, sweating, dilation of blood vesselsand metabolic activities. Thisincreases the maintenance energy requirementsand change the partitioning of energy and nutrients away from growth, lactation and reproductive functions (Sejian et al., 2012). As more energy and nutrients are used to regulate body temperature and other physiological functions, less energy will be available for the productive pathways, including tissue growth, milk synthesis and reproductive performance. Further, heat stress reduces feed consumption, impaired rumen functioning, hormonal imbalances and poor follicle growth and conception (Nardone et al., 2010).Therefore, one of the main goals of climate resilient production is the selection of animals that achieve physiological homeostasis at a reduced metabolic cost of adaptation.Minimizing such production losses calls for both short-term measures as well as long-term genetic improvements.Nutritional strategies such as increased energy density in feed, rumen fermentation, antioxidant protectionand nutrient availability are important in maintaining production processes during feed shortages while proper reproduction management will reduce fertility losses due to thermal stress. These measures however, need continuous implementation and their efficacy is also dependent on environmental factors and resources. However, genetic improvement can be considered as a better strategy asdesirable adaptive characteristics can be accumulated and transferred over the generations (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). Therefore, selection of goats with thermotolerance, combined with growth and milk/meat production, efficient utilization of feed and reproductive ability, can result in the improvement of productivity without impairing their adaptation to climatic stress.

9.     A New Framework for Climate-Resilient Goat Production

Breeding climate resilient goats will involve integration of genetics, nutrition, animal management and continuous evaluation of animal’s performance instead of relying on one approach.The process may start with the conservation and characterization of indigenous goat populations,and further identifying animals that have combined climate resilience and desired production and reproduction traits.Nutritional, reproductive, health and farm management systems can subsequently be developed to meet the needs of these animals for particular climatic and production situations. Further, adopting precision livestock technologies can complement these strategies through the constant documentation of environmental exposures and responses of the animals, including behavioral, physiological and productive responses.This will serve as the basis to switch from herd-wide management strategies to individual-based strategies.Importantly, the approach needs to be adaptive and iterative. Data obtained from phenotyping and farm-level performance could be used to feed back into breeding and management programs in order to determine which animals, management approachesand practices have proven their consistency in various climatic regimes.These data could be used to fine tune selection protocols, to assess management approaches and to discover genotype by environment interactions which impact the animal’s performance.Further, repeated measures over time can differentiate between resilient and consistently high-performing individuals from those that perform only in favorable climates. Eventually, incorporating animal performance data with environmental and production data will help increase the resilience prediction and lead to more precise breeding, nutritional and management decisions.

10.  Conclusion & Future perspectives

Goats have high tolerance for heat and have developed a range of physiological, behavioral, and genetic adaptations that help them survive in extreme environments. Adaptation mechanisms such as regulation of body temperature, utilizing diverse and low-quality sources of food, conservation of water and physiological stability form the basis for their survival in challenging climatic environments. However, there is significant variation among the goat population, with indigenous goats serving as an important contributor of adaptive genetic diversity. Recent breakthroughs in the field of omics have shed light on the molecular mechanisms underlying goat adaptation, with developments in nutrition, management practices and precision livestock farming has complemented these efforts to evaluate and enhance the adaptive responses to climatic stressors. These developments provide a firmer foundation for understanding and enhancing the ability of goats to maintain their health and productivity in response to changes in climate conditions

However, future research has to focus on several areas which remain insufficiently explored. It is necessary to study the long-term impacts of multiple and combined climatic stressors instead of single heat-stress events because animals experience heat stress, food scarcity, water stress and disease pressure simultaneously. Seasonal and field-based experiments should be carried out in order to get a clear understanding of genotype by environment interaction and whether the resilience biomarkers established in laboratory experiments persist under farm conditions. Further, studies focusing on genomic and multi-omics information integration with sensor-based data should be performed as it may improve the selection accuracy of resilient goats that maintain stable performance under climatic stress. Alongside, economic analysis is also needed for these strategies to identify whether the enhanced resilience contributes to economic gains in terms of increased productivity and profitability. Further, designing climate-resilient production models tailored to specific agro-ecological regions is also essential for addressing local climatic and production challenges. These efforts could aid in sustaining the adaptive and productive potential of goats thereby, ensuring sustainable livestock production and food security in changing climate scenarios.

titles.title: Goats in a Warming World: Mechanisms of Climate Resilience and Strategies for Sustainable Production

descriptions.description:
Abstract

Goats are well adapted to environmental stress and possess superior thermotolerance potential that enables them to perform under extreme temperatures, limited feed and water availability and other challenging conditions. Their resilience potential is associated with physiological, behavioural and genetic characteristics that allows them to tolerate harsh conditions however, the expression of these traits differs among breeds and individual animals. Among the goat populations, indigenous goat breeds are valuable because of generations of adaptation to local environments have shaped genetic diversity that can contribute to future climate-resilient breeding programs. At the molecular level, genomics and other omics studies are providing insights into the biological and molecular processes associated with these adaptive responses. However, the ability to withstand environmental stress does not always ensure maintenance of production, since increased thermoregulatory demands can alter nutrient partitioning and reduces the resources available for growth, reproduction, milk and meat production. Nutritional and management interventions can help minimize these production losses however, genetic interventions can provide permanent solution by combining adaptive capacity with desirable productive traits over generations. Further, Precision livestock farming (PLF) technologies support this process by enabling continuous monitoring of animal behaviour, physiology and environmental exposure. Such efforts facilitate the identification and selection of goats that remain healthy and productive under climatic stress thereby, strengthening the basis for sustainable production and food security in increasingly variable environments.

Keywords: Climate change; Goats; indigenous breeds; omics technologies; PLF; resilience  

 

1.     Introduction: The Goat as a Climate-Resilient Livestock Species

As the global population continues to grow rapidly, there will be an increasing demand for animal-source foods to ensure the constant food supply to the growing human population. However, climate change is altering the livestock production as the conditions that would favor livestock productivity is becoming hostile. The increasing temperature, reduced availability of water, reduction in grazing land and increased climatic variability significantly impacts the productivity, reproductivity and welfare of animals (Sejian et al., 2018). Under these circumstances, livestock species that have lower requirements but remain productive will be the key players in ensuring global food securityAmong livestock species, goats have remarkable adaptation to climatic conditions as they can survive in different climatic zones including the Sahara Desert where temperatures rise above 45°C, as well as high altitude regions such as the Himalayas above 4,000 meters, tropical rainforest regions and semi-arid drought prone areas (Danso et al., 2024). They play a significant role in contributing to global food security through production of meat, milk, fiber, hides and manure, as well as being an important source of income to millions of poor farmers (Sejian et al., 2018). 

The ability of goats to withstand the harsh climatic changes is due to the fact that they possess unique attributes in terms of morphology, physiology, behavior and genetics. The small body size, thermoregulation capacity, browsing behavior, lower water requirement and their capability to feed on low-quality feed allows goats to remain productive under adverse and limited climatic conditions (Nair et al., 2021). The advancement in next-generation sequencing technologies and omics platforms have played an enormous role in gaining insight into the molecular mechanisms of these adaptation capabilities, which has assisted in identifying the genes and biomarkers for climate-resilient breeding (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). Additionally, integrating with the emerging precision livestock farming enables real-time evaluation of animal health, well-being and environmental reactions, thus leading to more accurate and climate-smart management practices (Rebez et al., 2024). This chapter focuses on the effects of climatic stressors on goat production systems, as well as the biology, genetics, and molecular adaptations in goats that allows them to cope up with the challenging environments. In addition, the chapter discusses the inclusion of indigenous genetic resources, application of multi-omics approaches, precision livestock farming, and climate-smart approaches for formulating a holistic strategy for goat production.

2.     Climate Stressors Shaping the Future of Goat Production

Climate change is modifying the environmental circumstances that have made goat farming successful previously. The increase in ambient temperature, increased and persistent heat waves, irregular precipitation, persistent droughts and extreme weather conditions have become a common phenomenon (Sejian et al., 2018).These changes are not only intensifying thermal stress but are also affecting the availability of feeds and water, vegetation development, and the distribution of pasturelands (Nardone et al., 2010).In many arid and semi-arid areas, climate changes have contributed to desertification, decrease in the availability of food and increase in competition for natural resources.With the intensification of these climate changes even the goats withsuperior adaptive abilityare facing greater challenges in maintaining their health and productivity.

The climatic stressors have significant effects on goat health, well-being and productivity. Among these stressors, heat stress is considered to be the most detrimental affecting the physiological processes by elevating body temperature, respiration rateand water intake while decreasing feed intake and nutrient absorption.Further, long-term heat exposure will adversely affect the growth performance, reproduction, milk productivity, immunity and kid survival rate (Cheng et al., 2022). At the same time, feed shortage caused by drought also results in reduced quantity and quality of pasture, thereby making the goats rely on browsing of poor-quality feed that might fail to satisfy the nutritional needs of the goats.Water scarcity further compounds these problems as it impacts metabolic functions, thermoregulationand the performance of animals.In addition to these direct effects, climate change hinders livestock production through their indirect effects by altering feed resources, grazing ecosystem and the distribution of parasites and infectious diseases (Lacetera et al., 2019).Thus, climatic factors decrease productivity and make goat farming systems more vulnerable especially in the developing countries.

3.     The Biology of Goat Resilience: Why Do Some Goats Cope Better?

Goat’s ability to survive climatic stress differs considerably between breeds, even among the individuals of same breed and production system (Renaudeau et al., 2012).Some goats resist and perform normally in terms of growth, reproduction, milk production and immune system functioning in hot conditions, while other goats fail to resist the climatic conditions and thus their performances deteriorate significantly. This resistance to climatic stress depends on the adaptation ability of these goats, which is influenced by genetics, environmental exposure, physiological plasticity, nutrition and adaptation to the local climatic condition (Sejian et al., 2018). Consequently, indigenous goats are usually more tolerant to climatic stress because they have been evolving for generations in either hot, dry, or mountainous climates and the generations of exposure to the unfavorable environmental condition have allowed positive selection for beneficial alleles and regulatory mechanism that help goats survive under climatic stress (Sejian et al., 2021). Therefore, climate resilience is not a single trait but rather a combination of many biological mechanisms that act together to ensure normal body functioning amid stressful environmental conditions.

The adaptation of goats to climate depends on the combined effect of the physiological, behavioral, endocrine, and molecular processes to counteract the impact of environmental stress. Physiological thermoregulation through sweating, panting, vasodilation of blood vessels and metabolic heat reduction, as well as behavioral adaptation of the animals like seeking for shade and altering grazing behaviour are helpful in thermoregulation. These mechanisms are further aided by efficient water use, feeding of poor quality feedstuffs and metabolic plasticity that enable the goats to maintain their physiological functions despite being exposed to heat and nutritional stresses for a prolonged period (Nair et al., 2021). Hormonal regulation through cortisol and thyroid hormones additionally regulates metabolism in accordance with requirements of the environment, while increased expression of heat shock proteins and antioxidant enzymes ensures protection of cells against oxidative stress, stabilization of proteins, and cell viability (Nair et al., 2021). At the molecular level, these adaptation processes occur through the interplay of several genes that are associated with thermoregulation, immune system, energy balance, hydration and cell maintenance. The expression of these genes are further influenced by several factors like environmental conditions, nutrition, epigenetic mechanisms, host-microbiome relationship and management practices (Abioja et al., 2023). Consequently, these mechanisms define the climate resilience in goats and can be used as a basis for improving breeding, nutrition and farm management.

4.     The Multi-Omics Architecture of Climate Resilience 

Climate resilience in goats cannot be comprehensively understood through research on one particular gene or biological process since each level of biology plays an important role in the adaptation process. Omics technologies have greatly transformed climate resilience studies because of their ability to allow for the analysis of diverse biological elements, including genes, transcripts, proteins, metabolites and microbes. These approaches help gain insights into the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying adaptation thereby, providing a deeper understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying climate resilience. The different layers of omics offer different aspects of the biological puzzle. Genetic variation is one of the key determinants of climate resilience in goats and genomics has been extensively applied to study genes and genomic loci for heat resistance, immune responses, energy metabolism and other climate resilient traits (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). However, the activity of genes undergo constant changes due to environmental stress and transcriptomics has made possible to gain useful information about the genes and pathways regulated in response to stressful conditions (Shashank et al., 2024). The effect of the environment on gene expression has also been studied by epigenomics which revealed epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation, histone modifications and non-coding RNAs are involved in adaptive plasticity without changing the DNA sequence (Aravindh et al., 2025). Similarly, proteomics and metabolomics have increased our knowledge on the functional and metabolic changes related to cellular defense, antioxidative defense, immune system, tissue regeneration and energy metabolism under climatic stress conditions (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). Furthermore, research on the microbiome has emphasized the importance of rumen and gut microflora in increasing the efficiency of nutrition, metabolism, immune response, and methane regulation (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). However, the real strength of these technologies is harnessed through a multi-omics strategy. Multi-omics technology integrates information from the genome, transcriptome, epigenome, proteome, metabolome and microbiome to encompass the complexity of the interaction process during the adaptation process. This can aid in providing a better understanding of climate adaptation mechanisms thereby, identifying biomarkers and pathways that can be used in breeding and management programs (Xiong et al., 2025).

5.     Indigenous Goat Breeds: Nature's Climate-Resilience Laboratory

Indigenous breeds of goats are considered as important genetic pools containing adaptive diversity resulting from thousands of years of selection for survival in diverse agroecological environments.While commercial breeds have mostly been selected under well-managed conditions for their superior production, indigenous goat breeds have been selected in an environment of prolonged heat stress, periodic shortage of feed and water, difficult topography and disease prevalence. This process of natural selection has resulted in selection of goats that could maintain their physiological stability, reproduction and productivity in an environmentally constrained situation.As a result, indigenous goat breeds exhibit a wide range of adaptive characteristics, such as heat resistance, reduced maintenance energy requirements, greater ability to digest low-quality forages, water conservation and disease resistance. Although indigenous goats are often more tolerant of adverse conditions than most commercial goat breeds, the adaptive ability varies widely even among different indigenous breeds (Nair et al., 2021). The adaptive potential of animals varies based on the environment under which each goat breed evolvesresulting in varying thermoregulatory capabilities, metabolic efficiency, endocrine response, immunity and cellular stress resistance.Such breed differences have been established through comparative studies.According to Pragna et al. (2018) there was a notable difference between the growth performance, growth hormone leveland IGF-1 expression among Salem Black, Osmanabadi, and Malabari goats in summer conditions, showing differences in their tolerance towards thermal stress. In a similar study, Aleena et al. (2018) showed better thermos physiological response and better HSP70 expression pattern in Salem Black goats than Osmanabadi and Malabari goats, thereby showing higher cellular protection in case of thermal stress.Such findings indicate the fact that the degree of resilience to climate changes differs between indigenous breeds of goats and depends on their adaptation to local environmental conditions.Consequently, naturally selected adaptive traits in indigenous goats play an essential role in providing genetic base for developing climate resilient production systems. The conservation of these indigenous populations is important for the preservation of the valuable adaptive traits and genetic resources.However, attempts should also be directed towards improving the productive capacity of the breeds without changing their high thermotolerance and adaptability potential.Such an approach will aid in breeding goats that will be both productive and adaptive, thereby guaranteeing sustainable livestock production.

6.     Enhancing Goat Resilience: From Natural Adaptation to Precision Intervention

Natural adaptation is an important basis for resilience however, it may fail to provide adequate resilience if the frequency or intensity of climatic stress continues to increase. Improving resilience thus involves a combination of genetic, nutritional and management approaches that help build on the innate adaptability of the animal (Sejian et al., 2018). Genetic selection programs can be employed in selecting animals that have the ability to withstand heat stresses while having superior growth, milk, meat and reproductive performance (Renaudeau et al., 2012). Nutritional approaches like antioxidants, minerals, phytogenic plants, probiotics, and bioactive feed ingredients can play a key role in maintaining metabolic function, immunity, and ruminal function under stressful conditions. Managemental approaches are equally important and include provision of shade and ventilation, availability of good water, alteration in grazing and feeding times to avoid exposure during the hot periods and altering stocking rates depending on pastures and climate (Prates, 2025). The development of precision technology presents an opportunity for making these interventions timely and animal specific. Wearable sensors, automatic thermal cameras, environment sensors, and digital monitoring tools may constantly monitor the changes in body temperature, respiration, physical activities, consumption of food and water, and the climate conditions surrounding the animals (Idowu and Idowu, 2026). The above data can help detect any early signs of heat stress or other forms of environmental stress even before the onset of any obvious production losses, helping farmers to react by altering the feeding regime, drinking water, providing shade or even rehousing them. Further, when integrated with genetic data and nutritional information, these technologies will aid in making more accurate decisions for both individual animals and entire herds (Idowu and Idowu, 2026).

7.     Digital and Precision Goat Farming: Measuring Resilience in Real Time 

Technological improvements in sensor-based technologies have made it possible to track the changes in behavior and physiological responses of goats in conjunction with the environmental parameters in real time. Continuous monitoring offers a greater chance of understanding the responses and recovery of goats during climatic stress. Wearable accelerometers have been employed to monitor movement and identify different behaviours like grazing, browsing, walking and resting period of the animal. Moreau et al. (2009) illustrated the usage of tri-axial accelerometers for automated identification of grazing behaviour in goats under different production systems. The GPS-based technique gives additional information on the distance of movement, grazing behaviour and location (Chebli et al., 2022). For instance, accelerometers together with GPS has been employed to determine the amount of time spent on grazing by dairy goats, thus highlighting the benefits of this approach in measuring the behaviour response in field conditions. Additionally, the use of infrared thermography gives an additional tool for non-invasive measurement of surface temperature and the environmental sensors provides continuous monitoring of temperature, humidity and heat load. Changes in eye temperature in Blanca Serrana goats have been reported by Bartolomé et al. (2019) during a stressful situation, confirming its potential value as a non-invasive parameter of physiological stress. Emerging technologies like automated video analysis and audio monitoring are also being investigated for continuous measurement of feeding, ruminating, and behavioral characteristics. All these technologies provide for multiple objective recordings, which, in turn, can serve as a tool to help assess an individual’s response to stress factors. Such technologies provide continuous readings which assist in evaluating the response of individual goats to environmental stress. Repetitive observations may further aid in differentiating animals having varying degrees of resilience. Correlating such responses with growth, milk production, reproduction, health and genetics data can enhance the process of selecting goats that retain their productive potential even under stressed climates.

8.     Sustainable Production: Moving Beyond Survival Toward Productivity

Animal's ability to tolerate climatic stressors may not automatically mean sustained productivity.Under heat stress conditions, goats resort to various thermoregulation strategies such as increased respiration rate, sweating, dilation of blood vesselsand metabolic activities. Thisincreases the maintenance energy requirementsand change the partitioning of energy and nutrients away from growth, lactation and reproductive functions (Sejian et al., 2012). As more energy and nutrients are used to regulate body temperature and other physiological functions, less energy will be available for the productive pathways, including tissue growth, milk synthesis and reproductive performance. Further, heat stress reduces feed consumption, impaired rumen functioning, hormonal imbalances and poor follicle growth and conception (Nardone et al., 2010).Therefore, one of the main goals of climate resilient production is the selection of animals that achieve physiological homeostasis at a reduced metabolic cost of adaptation.Minimizing such production losses calls for both short-term measures as well as long-term genetic improvements.Nutritional strategies such as increased energy density in feed, rumen fermentation, antioxidant protectionand nutrient availability are important in maintaining production processes during feed shortages while proper reproduction management will reduce fertility losses due to thermal stress. These measures however, need continuous implementation and their efficacy is also dependent on environmental factors and resources. However, genetic improvement can be considered as a better strategy asdesirable adaptive characteristics can be accumulated and transferred over the generations (Kalaignazhal et al., 2024). Therefore, selection of goats with thermotolerance, combined with growth and milk/meat production, efficient utilization of feed and reproductive ability, can result in the improvement of productivity without impairing their adaptation to climatic stress.

9.     A New Framework for Climate-Resilient Goat Production

Breeding climate resilient goats will involve integration of genetics, nutrition, animal management and continuous evaluation of animal’s performance instead of relying on one approach.The process may start with the conservation and characterization of indigenous goat populations,and further identifying animals that have combined climate resilience and desired production and reproduction traits.Nutritional, reproductive, health and farm management systems can subsequently be developed to meet the needs of these animals for particular climatic and production situations. Further, adopting precision livestock technologies can complement these strategies through the constant documentation of environmental exposures and responses of the animals, including behavioral, physiological and productive responses.This will serve as the basis to switch from herd-wide management strategies to individual-based strategies.Importantly, the approach needs to be adaptive and iterative. Data obtained from phenotyping and farm-level performance could be used to feed back into breeding and management programs in order to determine which animals, management approachesand practices have proven their consistency in various climatic regimes.These data could be used to fine tune selection protocols, to assess management approaches and to discover genotype by environment interactions which impact the animal’s performance.Further, repeated measures over time can differentiate between resilient and consistently high-performing individuals from those that perform only in favorable climates. Eventually, incorporating animal performance data with environmental and production data will help increase the resilience prediction and lead to more precise breeding, nutritional and management decisions.

10.  Conclusion & Future perspectives

Goats have high tolerance for heat and have developed a range of physiological, behavioral, and genetic adaptations that help them survive in extreme environments. Adaptation mechanisms such as regulation of body temperature, utilizing diverse and low-quality sources of food, conservation of water and physiological stability form the basis for their survival in challenging climatic environments. However, there is significant variation among the goat population, with indigenous goats serving as an important contributor of adaptive genetic diversity. Recent breakthroughs in the field of omics have shed light on the molecular mechanisms underlying goat adaptation, with developments in nutrition, management practices and precision livestock farming has complemented these efforts to evaluate and enhance the adaptive responses to climatic stressors. These developments provide a firmer foundation for understanding and enhancing the ability of goats to maintain their health and productivity in response to changes in climate conditions

However, future research has to focus on several areas which remain insufficiently explored. It is necessary to study the long-term impacts of multiple and combined climatic stressors instead of single heat-stress events because animals experience heat stress, food scarcity, water stress and disease pressure simultaneously. Seasonal and field-based experiments should be carried out in order to get a clear understanding of genotype by environment interaction and whether the resilience biomarkers established in laboratory experiments persist under farm conditions. Further, studies focusing on genomic and multi-omics information integration with sensor-based data should be performed as it may improve the selection accuracy of resilient goats that maintain stable performance under climatic stress. Alongside, economic analysis is also needed for these strategies to identify whether the enhanced resilience contributes to economic gains in terms of increased productivity and profitability. Further, designing climate-resilient production models tailored to specific agro-ecological regions is also essential for addressing local climatic and production challenges. These efforts could aid in sustaining the adaptive and productive potential of goats thereby, ensuring sustainable livestock production and food security in changing climate scenarios.
